response.title: Why does nylon filament come out stringy and weak, and do I need a dryer that feeds the printer while it prints?
response.answer:
Moisture is the most likely reason your nylon filament is coming out stringy and weak. Nylon (PA) is extremely hygroscopic, meaning it absorbs water from the air. Even a spool that looks dry can contain enough moisture to cause printing problems.

And yes, printing directly from a filament dryer is highly recommended for nylon, especially for long prints. But it's not always necessary.

1. Why nylon prints stringy and weak

Wet filament

Water inside the filament turns into steam in the hot nozzle, causing inconsistent extrusion, bubbles, stringing, and poor layer bonding. You might hear popping or sizzling.

Poor layer adhesion

Moisture, low nozzle temperature, excessive cooling, or printing too fast can prevent layers from bonding properly. Parts may split along layer lines under stress.

Temperature and retraction problems

Nylon stays relatively fluid when hot. Excessive nozzle temperature, insufficient retraction, or slow travel moves can cause fine strings even with dry filament.

2. Do you need a dryer running while printing?

It depends on the print duration, humidity, and nylon formulation.

Printing situation

	

Recommendation




Short print, 1–2 hours

	

Pre-dry, then print from a dry box




Medium print, 3–6 hours

	

Dry box or active dryer recommended




Long print, 8–24 hours

	

Active dryer or well-sealed dry-feed system strongly recommended




Humid environment

	

Prefer continuous dry feeding




PA6 or highly moisture-sensitive nylon

	

Continuous dry feeding especially useful

Nylon can reabsorb moisture within hours in humid conditions, although the rate varies significantly by formulation and ambient humidity.

Important distinction: You don't necessarily need a heater running throughout the print. A properly sealed dry box with desiccant can keep pre-dried nylon dry while feeding the printer. An active dryer is useful when humidity is high or the spool hasn't been fully dried beforehand.

3. Recommended starting settings

These are general starting ranges, not universal settings. Your filament manufacturer's specifications should take priority.

Setting

	

Starting point




Drying temperature

	

70–90°C, if spool and filament permit




Drying duration

	

6–12 hours, potentially longer




Nozzle temperature

	

250–290°C




Bed temperature

	

70–100°C




Part cooling fan

	

0–20%




Print speed

	

30–60 mm/s initially




Enclosure

	

Strongly recommended




Dry-box humidity

	

Ideally below 15–20% RH

PA6, PA12, PA-CF, and other nylon blends can require substantially different settings. Some nylons need higher drying temperatures than typical consumer filament dryers can provide.

4. What I would do first

Dry the spool according to the manufacturer's temperature and time recommendations.

Print a small test part immediately after drying, ideally feeding from a dry box.

Check whether the popping, stringing, and weak layers disappear.

If the filament is still stringy, tune nozzle temperature and retraction.

If layers remain weak, check nozzle temperature, cooling, print speed, and enclosure temperature.

Don't try to fix wet nylon by increasing retraction alone. Drying it first is much more effective.

5. Two questions that would help me pinpoint your problem
What type of nylon are you printing?
PA6
PA12
PA-CF (carbon fiber nylon)
Not sure / other
What printer are you using?
How are you currently storing or drying the filament?
No dryer, exposed to room air
Dry before printing
Print directly from an active dryer
Print from a sealed dry box
Get recommended settings

With those details, I can tell you whether a continuously heated dryer is worth buying or whether a sealed dry box will be enough.
